title: 9/9/2026 | MARK FRIESENHAHN | BR | Response to Oncor's 09/02/26 Exception Brief. Deny the CCN Amendment for Docket 59475

documents.text:
=== Mark Friesenhahn response to Oncors Exception Brief and recommendation to AJLs and PUC 090926.pdf ===
1
 Introduction
Administrative Law Judges and PUC Commissioners, my name is Mark Friesenhahn,
intervenor on Docket 59475. I have been heavily involved in this process, including review
of TSP, ERCOT and other studies that underpinned the basis for the proposed 765 kV
powerlines and the TSP CCN amendment requests.


Summary
To get straight to my concerns and main point:

I strongly object to Oncor and LCRA’s Exception Brief. The ALJs should “hold their
ground” on the PFD recommending denial and the PUC should do the ethical and right
thing; deny the CCN amendment.

Oncor/LCRA submitted 81 pages of what I, as a 5th generation Texas, a pecan farm and
landowner a ected by the proposed 765 kV powerlines, call a lot of legal “gobbly-goop”
that is intended to confuse and discourage involved parties, burden the ALJs with long and
complicated documents, and detract from the main issue: we need generation, not all of
the 765 kV powerlines.

This is not surprising, since the TSPs stand to gain 9-10% proﬁt on $33 billion dollars or the
actual cost, expected to be much higher. They have a large incentive to push for CCN
amendment approval. On the farm, we call that “the fox guarding the chick house”. Not to
mention that Oncor’s brief is wrong on many accounts—more on that in a minute.


Recommendation
The PUC should

1) Pause and reevaluate/reassess the need for the proposed 765-kV transmission lines
included in the STEP report (Texas Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan,

2) Take a hard look at these assessments and use the legislature’s numerous requests &
letters to support the pause,

3). Add assessment of generation needs, including in the Permian Basin (BP), in the
reevaluation

4). Address apparent transmission bottlenecks in the PB immediately

Do the ethical and right thing: deny the CCN amendments.



                                               2
 The correct and obvious answer: The NEEDS DETERMINATION for the entire proposed 765
kV powerline plan is inadequate, deﬁcient and ﬂawed, and does not meet statuary
requirements. Studies addressed HOW to transmit SOME of the forecast electric power to
the PB (The forecast is largely driven by Data Center power forecast demand which is
changing rapidly) but, studies did not include a full assessment of ADDITIONAL POWER
GENERATION needed and WHERE IT NEEDS TO BE LOCATED, nor ALTERNATIVES to
generate power on-site in the Permian Basin.

PUC Chairman Gleason testiﬁed that the powerlines are needed to support Permian Basin
oil & gas operations. He conveniently left out that data centers and other non-oil & gas
industries account for over 80% of the demand forecast. Forecasts that were conveniently
supplied by the TSPs via “Attestation Letters”. Letters that were overinﬂated, causing
ERCOT to reduce the estimates to 27% of that submitted. The 27% still adds to over 80% of
the PB load forecast.

Strategically, the plan involves multi-billion-dollar extension cords without consideration of
generators to feed the extension cords.

Why does everyone except the TSPs and PUC see this? Proﬁt, not the correct sensible
solution is the answer.


Details
The following was compiled by several involved parties. It is detailed but supportive of
our recommendation.

The PFD focus primarily on the ﬁndings that were determinative in the ALJs'
recommendation of denial, namely that Applicants failed to establish the need for the
Import Path 2 Projects and failed to comply with the Commission's rules concerning public
participation meetings and notice of the Project Application. We agree fully with the ALJs.

Oncor and LCRA TSC submitted their exceptions to the PFD (Exceptions Brief) on
Wednesday, September 2, 2026. The applicants argue that "...the PBRP alone is su icient
to establish the need for the recommended 765kV transmission infrastructure." The
applicants further argue that ERCOT's recommendation provided in the PBRP is entitled to
"great weight" under the PUC's rules.

Involved parties completed a line-by-line comparison of the Oncor/LCRA TSC Exceptions
Brief to the PFD. The comparison found 101 exceptions that could be compared to the
PFD. Of the 101 exceptions:




                                              3
 - 33 Oncor/LCRA TSC exceptions misstate the ALJs' ﬁndings because the exceptions say
something that is not said in the PFD.

- 40 Oncor/LCRA TSC exceptions are incomplete because the exceptions omit facts in the
PFD, which changes the meaning of the ALJ's ﬁndings.

- 25 exceptions accurately state ﬁndings in the PFD, but this does not mean that Oncor's or
LCRA TSC's argument is accurate.

As a result of our comparison, it was concluded the Oncor & LCRA TSC Exceptions
Brief materially misstates the ALJs' ﬁndings and conclusions in the PFD. Following are
three important examples:

(1) "Great Weight" Misstates PUC Rule: The Oncor/LCRA TSC Exceptions Brief argues many
times that ERCOT's recommendation provided by the PBRP is entitled to "great weight"
under Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II). The Oncor and LCRA TSC Exceptions Brief misstates this
PUC Rule because the rule also says, "The forecasted load growth and additional load
currently seeking interconnection must be substantiated by quantiﬁable evidence of
projected load growth" before ERCOT's recommendation is given "great weight."

(2) S&P 2022 Oil & Gas Forecast: Signiﬁcant oil and gas producers engaged S&P Global to
prepare a 2022 study on the electriﬁcation of the Permian Basin. The ALJs found that
Oncor provided the S&P 2022 study to ERCOT and it was the only study used by ERCOT for
oil & gas forecasted load in the PBRP. The ALJs found that ERCOT did not verify or
independently evaluate the S&P 2022 Study, and the ALJs found evidence that exposes
ﬂaws in the S&P 2022 study. The Oncor/LCRA TSC Exceptions Brief does not disclose or
explain the ALJs ﬁndings about the S&P 2022 study in the PFD.

(3) Non-Oil & Gas Forecast: ERCOT relied on letters provided by o icers of Oncor and other
transmission service providers (TSPs) for 55% of the non-oil & gas forecasted load in the
PBRP. The ALJs found that Oncor/LCRA TSC did not verify the forecasts in the o icer's
letters, and the non-oil & gas forecast load was overstated and unsubstantiated. The ALJs
also found that ERCOT changed their load-forecasting methodology after the PBRP was
issued and these changes materially reduce the forecasted load in the PBRP. The
Oncor/LCRA TSC Exceptions Brief does not disclose that 55% of the non-oil & gas
forecasted load is based on letters provided by o icers of the TSPs or that Oncor/LCRA TSC
did not verify the forecasts in the o icer letters.

The ALJs acknowledge the PUC should give "great weight" to an ERCOT recommendation if
the projected load growth is "substantiated by quantiﬁable evidence of projected load
growth." But the ALJs found the non-oil & gas forecast, mostly provided by the TSPs, was
overstated and unsubstantiated, and ERCOT did not verify or independently evaluate the


                                             4
 S&P 2022 Study. The ALJs found the projected load growth was not substantiated by
quantiﬁable evidence. Therefore, the ALJs found ERCOT's PBRP recommendation should
not be given "great weight" by virtue of the PUC Rule and that "...the greater weight of the
credible evidence is against [ERCOT's] recommendation."

How can the PUC rely on the Oncor & LCRA TSC Exceptions Brief that materially
misstates the ALJ's ﬁndings and conclusions in the PFD?


Conclusion
The NEEDS DETERMINATION for the entire proposed 765 kV powerline plan is inadequate,
deﬁcient and ﬂawed, and does not meet statuary requirements.

The PUC should pause and reevaluate/reassess the need for the proposed 765-kV
transmission lines included in the STEP report (Texas Strategic Transmission Expansion
Plan), add assessment of generation needs, including in the Permian Basin (BP), in the
reevaluation and address apparent transmission bottlenecks in the PB immediately.

A number of Intervenors, legislators and industry advocacy groups share this
recommendation. Their view have been widely circulated.

Deny the CCN amendments.



Respectfully submitted,
Mark Friesenhahn
Comal Pecan Farm
231 High Creek Road
New Braunfels, TX 78132
281-660-5445
mark@comalpecanfarm.com
Texas PE License 41912
